listenings.text: I prepare people for rooms where somebody can say no, and I always start in the same place. Your first sentence does about half the work, and almost everybody wastes it. Most people use it to thank the room and explain the agenda. Do not do that. Use it to say what you want them to decide. Then three parts, in this order, and only three. One: the claim. One sentence, no more. Two: the evidence that backs it up, and by evidence I mean something a person in that room can check without asking you. Three, and this is the part that wins arguments: the consequence of not deciding. Not the benefits of deciding. The cost of waiting. And one last thing, about the objection you are most afraid of. Say it yourself, out loud, before anybody else does. An objection you name loses most of its power. An objection that catches you keeps all of it, and it takes the room with it.

I had two meetings that year that I still think about, and I lost one of them for a reason that had nothing to do with the numbers. The one I won, I opened with the decision. First sentence: I want a yes on this, today, and here is why. And then I said the objection myself, before anybody could raise it. We are late, this is expensive, and here is what happens if we wait. Twenty minutes, done. The one I lost, I had better data. Genuinely better. But the first person who pushed back caught me, and instead of answering I argued with him. My tone went defensive in about four seconds, and after that nobody in that room heard a single piece of my evidence, because they were all watching two people fight. So the sentence I use now, every time, is this one: that is a fair point, and here is what happens if we do nothing about it. It costs me nothing and it keeps the room.
